Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Artifacts: slides (https://redwood.app/decks/autoscale-orbit), sample trace upload link (s3://orbit-research/traces/2026-01), benchmark template (https://redwood.app/benchmarks/template)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive to align on autoscale behaviour, burst policy tradeoffs, queueing model assumptions, KV cache warmup impact, and quantization choices for Orbit's mixed chat+analysis workload. Goal: produce an actionable simulation and pilot plan to validate SLOs on reserved GPU pools + burst.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and constraints (VPC, egress, on-prem legal data)
- Burst profile and peak-to-median ratios
- Queueing/capacity model (M/M/c vs measured arrivals)
- KV cache hit dynamics during cold-starts and shard eviction
- Batching policies and tail-latency SLOs (P95/P99)
- Quantization tradeoffs: int8 vs fp16 and perf regressions on long context
- Failure/fallback policies: model variants and regional fallback
- Pilot plan and next steps

Transcript (timestamps are approximate, auto-transcribed - expect small errors):

[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm alex mercer, i'll run the commercial side. priya and diego are from our se team. john, maria, tom — thanks for taking the time. can you confirm we're still on the sample trace in s3?

[00:18] John (CTO): yeah, that's live. maria uploaded the trace last night, the 2-week sample. hey alex, priya. our main ask: how do we keep p95 under 250ms on chat while handling spikes to 8x baseline?

[00:32] Priya (SE): great, thanks john. quick clarifying q: when you say p95 for chat, is that for end-to-end including network, or just token generation? and what batch sizes are you typically seeing?

[00:45] Maria (Platform Eng): it's mostly end-to-end as seen by our API gateway, so includes a little network. typical token lengths are 60–120 tokens for chat, but we have long analytic jobs hitting 1.5k tokens sporadically. our baseline qps is ~120 req/s, peaks at 1k during campaign bursts.

[01:05] Alex: ok that mix explains the complexity — chat latency tight, long-context jobs heavy. priya, do you want to start with queueing model?

[01:12] Priya: sure. so we modeled two approaches: conservative reserved pool sized for 95th percentile sustained load, plus a burst queue that routes to pre-warmed ephemeral nodes. there's a tradeoff: bigger reserved units increases cost but reduces cold-start and queueing. we usually recommend a hybrid where reserved handles steady-state plus short bursts, ephemeral for large short spikes.

[01:35] Tom (SRE): how long does a kv cache warmup take on your runtime? we saw 20–30s cold tails during our early bench with kv mis-shard.

[01:48] Priya: warmup depends on key distribution. for stateful chat we see 1–3 tokens effective warmup for same-conversation prefix caching, but for cross-session it's larger — you can get 10s of ms to seconds if the kv needs to be repopulated from disk. also note our k-v cache is sometimes transcribed as "kay vee cache" in the auto notes, so apologies.

[02:10] Diego (Solutions Eng): to add: if workloads have high prefix locality (same user/conv), hit rates can be 70–90% after a few requests. if it's stateless batch, hit rates drop fast and batch-driven throughput becomes the limiting factor.

[02:27] Maria: our chat is sticky by user but we have lots of anonymous analysis jobs. those long jobs are the problem because they hold GPU for longer and block queues.

[02:40] Priya: that's where quantization can help: int8 reduces memory footprint and increases concurrency on the card, but you may see slight degeneration on some tasks. for long-context, int8 kernel perf can be worse in some fused ops — depends on model and kernel set. we recommend running a small eval suite.

[02:58] John: curious about batching — we thought bigger batch sizes always improve throughput but we care about tail. what's the right balance?

[03:08] Priya: batching increases throughput but can add head-of-line latency if you wait to fill a batch. our runtime supports latency-aware batching: we set a max wait time (5–10ms) and a max batch size. for chat we bias the policy towards low wait time; for analysis jobs we allow larger batches. there's also adaptive batching that changes with observed qps.

[03:28] Tom: so in a spike that ramps quickly to 8x, how do you avoid queue pile-up that kills p99?

[03:35] Priya: two levers: pre-warmed burst capacity and backpressure. pre-warmed pools are kept warm for short windows (we call them "surge absorbers") and are billed as ephemeral but ready. backpressure is applied at the gateway — we have prioritized queues: routing by route and token-cost. lower-priority analytic jobs can be queued or shed.

[03:58] Maria: what's the typical warm duration for surge absorbers? we can't keep them always warm on cost grounds.

[04:06] Diego: typically 2–7 minutes depending on your SLA for cold recovery. we simulate shutdown behavior too — there's a graceful drain to keep KV in-sync. cost models show keeping a small number pre-warmed is often cheaper than long tail latency penalties.

[04:24] John: can you walk through the queueing math you use? our folks are comfortable with M/M/c but our arrivals are bursty and not Poisson.

[04:33] Priya: yes — we start with M/M/c as a baseline to reason about utilization, but we use measured traces to drive a discrete-event simulator. that captures burstiness, correlated arrivals, and multi-route token variability. we also simulate with your exact token length histogram and model variants (fp16/int8) to estimate service time distributions.

[04:56] Maria: will the simulator include kv cache warmup? that's critical.

[05:02] Priya: yes. we model cache hit probability as a function of session affinity and recency. warmup periods increase the effective service time for early requests; we can also model sharded cache thawing with network transfer times if you use cross-node kv storage.

[05:20] Tom: regarding VPC/on-prem constraints: we need to ensure private data never leaves our VPC. can your dedicated offering be deployed in our VPC with KMS integration?

[05:30] Alex: yes — Redwood Private supports VPC peering and on-prem options. we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping. we'll share SOC2 + HSM notes in the security pack. note: our private plan still uses the same runtime features (batching, cache), but networking adds a few ms to network hops.

[05:50] Aisha (Data Scientist): about quantization — do you support per-channel int8 for our transformer? we tried quantizing and saw hallucination drift on some math tasks.

[06:00] Priya: per-channel int8 is supported for a subset of ops in our compilation path; sometimes we fall back to mixed precision for sensitive layers. hallucination can result from quantization noise; we recommend an eval set and a small A/B to verify quality. sometimes we keep fp16 on critical head layers.

[06:18] John: let's talk cost: if we reserve a small dedicated pool for baseline and rely on bursts for the 8x events, how do we price that?

[06:27] Alex: pricing will depend on commit term and size. typical pattern: reserve for 2–3x baseline and rely on ephemeral burst for the rest; we can give a blended hourly rate in the pilot pricing doc. i'll send an example.

[06:38] Maria: one of our constraints: our gateway enforces hard timeouts at 1s. if batching adds 50–100ms even up to 1s, that's risky.

[06:47] Priya: understood. so we should tune the latency-aware batching thresholds to target 150–200ms service time for chat requests. that gives headroom for network and retries.

[07:00] Diego: quick demo now — i'm going to share a simple sim of a 10-minute trace to show queue depth under three configs: reserved-only, reserved+burst, reserved+burst+sheding.

[07:12] [screen share starts — Diego]
[07:18] Diego: ok graph one shows queue depth over time. you can see when we use only reserved pool, queue depth spikes and p99 jumps. with burst pool, queue depth flattens but cost metric increases. with shedding low-priority jobs, p95 improves and cost is controlled.

[07:40] Maria: that looks promising. what's the assumed kv hit rate in the sim?

[07:46] Priya: for this run it's 55% initial, ramp to 80% within 30s for sessioned chat. we can change those params.

[07:55] Tom: the sim shows warmup time for new ephemerals of 45s — can you reduce that?

[08:02] Diego: warmup numbers are conservative; with preloaded model weights and a warmed kv snapshot we can drop to 12–18s. the larger cost is repopulating per-conversation KV state across shards which depends on your session affinity.

[08:20] John: do you do any KV prefetching on cold attach? like prefetch top-5 keys for active users?

[08:27] Priya: yes, we support prefix prefetch heuristics and priority loading. we can also keep an LRU of recent session keys in memory on the pool to reduce cold penalties. often this requires a short metadata sync at attach time.

[08:41] Maria: about shedding, can we prioritize by customer tier and route? our premium users must never be shed.

[08:48] Priya: absolutely — routing policy supports per-tenant priorities and per-route SLOs. during high load, we throttle or queue non-critical routes and send explicit 429s for best-effort work.

[09:00] Aisha: when you do benchmark runs, do you also check quality metrics? we need to make sure quantization doesn't reduce our Math Q/A accuracy below threshold.

[09:09] Diego: yes we run both latency/throughput and evals. we can run your math QA set and compare fp16 vs int8, report token-level differences and top-level accuracy.

[09:24] John: ok practical ask: can you run the sim on our trace with two configs: (A) reserve 3x baseline, int8 mixed for non-critical layers; (B) reserve 1.5x baseline + surge absorbers + shed low priority. we want p95 target <250ms and p99 <750ms.

[09:40] Priya: yes we can. action item for priya to run both sims and share results, plus a candidate quantization profile.

[09:48] Alex: on security, we'll share the SOC2 and KMS integration doc. maria, tom, any specific compliance red flags we should be aware of?

[09:57] Tom: we need audit logs for key material access, and proof that model weights never leave our VPC in private deployments. also need to confirm redwood's data retention windows.

[10:08] Alex: noted. we'll include audit log schema and retention options. our private deploy has options to ensure model artifacts are loaded from customer-controlled storage and keys are always customer-managed.

[10:22] Maria: network egress — we have strict egress rules and only a few whitelisted endpoints. will that block ephemeral nodes reaching the control plane?

[10:31] Diego: we can support a control-plane proxy that sits in your VPC or a partner appliance for air-gapped setups. that does add management overhead; we'll document it in the security pack.

[10:44] John: one more question about model variants: do you automatically fallback to smaller models when capacity is low? we want graceful reduction in quality rather than errors.

[10:55] Priya: yes, routing policies can define fallbacks. for example, reduce to a quantized variant or a smaller model family with known latency characteristics. we also support A/B style canary rollouts to test degradations.

[11:10] Maria: what's the visibility in console for token-level cost and per-route latency?

[11:16] Alex: Console gives per-route P95/P99, token-by-token cost breakdown, and tracing hooks to attach request IDs. we'll demo that in the follow-up.

[11:27] Aisha: about mixed workloads — analytic jobs with long token lengths skew utilization. can we evict long-running jobs preemptively during spikes?

[11:36] Priya: yes preemption policies are supported; long jobs can be checkpointed or resumed, or we can set a hard preemption threshold to reclaim capacity for chat. cost/quality tradeoff needs to be evaluated — preempting loses progress on long runs.

[11:50] John: ok let's move to pilot plan and timeline. we want a small pilot in feb to validate SLOs before committing reserved capacity.

[11:58] Alex: sounds good. proposed pilot scope: 4-week pilot with a small reserved pool (you choose 1.5x or 3x baseline) and a burst policy. we'll run sims, then a controlled traffic ramp, and measure p95/p99 + log quality metrics.

[12:12] Maria: for the controlled ramp, can you do a canary by tenant? we'd prefer to isolate premium tenants in the pilot.

[12:20] Alex: yes canary by tenant is standard. we'll work with your ops to define traffic slices.

[12:28] Diego: demo note — after the call i'll run a more realistic sim using your two-week trace, then produce a csv of p95/p99 per route under both configs. i'll attach the sim artifacts to the benchmark template.

[12:41] [screen share ends]

[12:46] Tom: small nit — we've seen model loading stalls when ephemeral nodes request checkpoints simultaneously; is there a recommended jitter?

[12:55] Priya: yes staggered attach with jitter and prefetching metadata is recommended; we also support prioritized attachment so critical nodes attach first.

[13:06] John: i have a question about prewarming cost amortization — is there an example ROI model? we'd like to see when prewarm beats latency penalties.

[13:16] Alex: we have a pricing workbook that models cost vs latency penalties. i'll send a pre-filled example with your baseline numbers. generally, if p99 penalties cost you more in conversion loss or SLA credits, prewarm is often worth it for a subset of capacity.

[13:30] Maria: any limitations with quantization on the custom ops we use? we use a fused attention kernel in our forked model.

[13:38] Priya: fused/custom ops can be an issue; sometimes we need to build custom kernel paths or keep those ops in fp16. we'd take that into account in the quantization profile and test on your model binary.

[13:52] Aisha: how do you surface quality regressions in the Console? do you have alerts?

[13:58] Diego: yes we have quality monitoring; you can define metric triggers (perplexity, BLEU, custom scoring) and get regression alerts tied to prompt sets. we also support per-deployment eval baselines.

[14:10] John: excellent. let's do the action items recap.

[14:15] Alex: recap: priya will run sims with the two configs and share csvs; diego will attach sim graphs and the benchmark template; alex will send pricing + security pack; maria will share traffic histograms; tom will confirm VPC/egress constraints. schedule follow-up week of 1/26.

[14:35] Maria: timeline sounds good. one more small ask — can you include an estimate of disk/network load from KV sync during bursts? we saw 250MB/s spikes in our in-house tests.

[14:45] Priya: yes we'll model network egress and disk. include your measured 250MB/s number in the sim input.

[14:55] John: thanks everyone. any final thoughts?

[15:00] Alex: thanks — big takeaway: hybrid reserved+burst with aggressive shedding of low-priority analytic jobs looks to be the most promising. we'll run sims and reconvene.

[15:10] Maria: thanks all.

[15:15] [meeting ends — recording stopped]
